a_rows_sample.anchor: P1: Situation = KnowledgeOS state ... P3: Reiter's delta completely defines KnowledgeOS delta ... P5: Reiter resolves KnowledgeOS equality ... P9: Golog is directly usable as the KnowledgeOS workflow model ... P10: progression is sufficient for KnowledgeOS state evolution. A failed correspondence is a valuable result.
a_rows_sample.statement: Full list of ten mandatory falsification-target propositions (P1-P10) spanning situation-identity, action-event correspondence, delta-completeness, Qualify-resolution, equality-resolution, history-completeness, provenance-necessity, knowledge-operator identity, Golog-as-workflow, and progression-sufficiency, with the explicit framing that a failed correspondence is itself a valuable research result.

a_rows_sample.anchor: P1: Situation = KnowledgeOS state | [TEST] | History \neq state ... P3: Reiter's delta completely defines KnowledgeOS delta | [TEST] | Missing authority, evidence ... P9: Golog is directly usable as KnowledgeOS workflow | [TEST] | Composition only
a_rows_sample.statement: Restates the ten P1-P10 falsification propositions from S2538, each pre-annotated [TEST] with a one-line expected-evidence hint (e.g. P1: History!=state; P3: missing authority/evidence; P8: different semantics; P9: composition only; P10: non-monotonic issues) -- these are hints guiding the test, not yet the executed test results.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Is `Qualify` a **precondition**? | **REFUTED** -- `P4`. `Poss(a,s)` gates *whether an action may occur*; `Qualify` concerns *whether a qualification holds of a knowledge item*. Different type, different pipeline position | **REFUTED**
a_rows_sample.statement: Negative test P4 (Reiter solves Qualify) is applied and Qualify-as-precondition is REFUTED: Reiter's Poss(a,s) gates whether an action may occur, while Qualify concerns whether a qualification holds of a knowledge item -- a different type occupying a different pipeline position, so the correspondence fails.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Identity / Equality | UNRESOLVED -- cannot be placed | equiv_sem is OPEN; placing it now would decide it by implication ... Observation | UNRESOLVED | OPEN in v1.2; see 07 ... Qualification | UNRESOLVED | P4 refuted the Poss identification ... Four of six cannot be placed. Recording that is the result; guessing would be the error.
a_rows_sample.statement: Of the six candidate components tested for inside/outside placement relative to the transition mechanism, four (Identity/Equality, Observation, Qualification, plus one more per the table) remain UNRESOLVED and cannot be placed without deciding open questions (equiv_sem OPEN, Observation OPEN in v1.2, Qualification's Poss-identification already refuted by P4) by implication; recording the four as unplaced is treated as the correct result, not a gap to be guessed shut.

a_rows_sample.anchor: verdict: Situation = K_t REFUTED -- and refuted by KnowledgeOS's OWN prior evidence, not by Reiter. 9 of 10 negative tests refuted. One BOUNDED candidate (delta as an SSA), one SUPPORTED mechanism (regression), one method, one naming. NO open item closed. Theory v1.2 unchanged; no governance act.
a_rows_sample.statement: Top-line verdict of the whole Reiter/KnowledgeOS derivation programme: Situation=K_t is REFUTED, and refuted by KnowledgeOS's own prior evidence rather than by anything in Reiter; 9 of 10 negative tests (P1-P10) are refuted; the programme yields one BOUNDED candidate (delta as a successor-state-axiom shape), one SUPPORTED mechanism (regression), one CORROBORATED method, and one NEW-SYNTHESIS naming; no open item is closed, Theory v1.2 is unchanged, and no governance act was taken.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Negative tests -- 9 of 10 refuted ... None fails because Reiter is wrong. Each fails because a construct is well-defined relative to assumptions KnowledgeOS does not satisfy -- causal completeness, consistent effect axioms, factive knowledge, an existing action theory. Reiter's machinery is available exactly to the extent that KnowledgeOS supplies the assumptions it requires -- and those assumptions are precisely the programme's open items.
a_rows_sample.statement: Meta-level interpretation of the 9-of-10 negative-test refutation: no test fails because Reiter's formalism is wrong: each fails because the relevant Reiter construct is well-defined only relative to assumptions KnowledgeOS does not (yet) satisfy -- causal completeness, consistent effect axioms, factive knowledge, and an existing action theory. Reiter's machinery is therefore available exactly to the extent KnowledgeOS supplies the assumptions it requires, and those assumptions are precisely the programme's remaining open items.

a_rows_sample.anchor: A subject matter pi is a set of atomic sentences. ... e\models O(\pi)\alpha \iff e|_\pi\models O\alpha ... A clause c is a prime implicate of phi iff \models(\phi\supset c) and for no proper subset c' is \models(\phi\supset c') ... P(\phi,\pi) is the conjunction of prime implicates of phi that mention pi.
a_rows_sample.statement: Full formal Only-Knowing-About O(pi) apparatus: subject matter pi as a set of atomic sentences, e-pi-minimal clauses restricting e to e|_pi, and the prime-implicate theorem relating O(pi)-knowledge to the conjunction of prime implicates of phi mentioning pi; proposed as the formal basis for focused queries, relevance, and Boundary (what is known vs not known about a topic).

b_rows_sample.anchor: This is much more valuable to KnowledgeOS than the extraction's simplistic statement: "Only-knowing = Zero." It isn't. Instead: KnowledgeAbout(K,\pi) ... K|_{\pi} ... our canonical projection was a structural projection; K|_pi is a subject-matter epistemic restriction. We should not conflate them.
b_rows_sample.statement: Rejects S2532's 'Only-knowing = Zero' as simplistic, proposing instead KnowledgeAbout(K,pi) / K|_pi as a subject-matter epistemic restriction, explicitly distinguished from the project's existing structural projection pi_K(K_t) (must not be conflated) -- a candidate research mechanism for Boundary.

b_rows_sample.anchor:
the strongest contribution is not "Only-knowing = Zero" or "TELL/ASK = KnowledgeOS kernel." The real contribution is: Explicit Representation -> Reasoning -> Derived Knowledge plus Query 
eq Evaluation 
eq Determination and Logical Closure

eq Global Knowledge State and finally Successor-State/Persistence Semantics
b_rows_sample.statement: Final verdict: the book fills missing parts of KnowledgeOS theory substantially, but the strongest contribution is NOT 'Only-knowing=Zero' or 'TELL/ASK=kernel' (both explicitly rejected earlier in this file) but rather the combination Explicit-Representation->Reasoning->Derived-Knowledge, Query!=Evaluation!=Determination, LogicalClosure!=OperationallyAvailableKnowledge, Subject-Matter-Boundary!=GlobalKnowledgeState, and Successor-State/Persistence Semantics as a serious formal basis for delta.

Note: Corrects the naive 'Only-knowing = Zero' claim: only-knowing-about gives a candidate KnowledgeAbout(K,pi) / epistemic projection K|_pi onto a subject matter, explicitly distinguished from the project's existing STRUCTURAL projection pi_K(K_t) -- the two must not be conflated; a candidate research mechanism for Boundary, not a definition of Zero (OnlyKnowing -> Zero candidate, not OnlyKnowing=Zero).

a_rows_sample.anchor: The fundamental problem ... P\land\neg P ... principle of explosion ... P,\neg P\vdash Q for arbitrary Q, the Knowledge State becomes useless. KnowledgeOS must tolerate contradiction without logical explosion.
a_rows_sample.statement: Requires KnowledgeOS tolerate contradiction (P∧¬P) without classical logical explosion (P,¬P⊢Q for arbitrary Q), since explosion would make the Knowledge State useless.

a_rows_sample.anchor: First distinction: contradiction versus inconsistency ... Contradiction ... Conflict(A_1,A_2,Ctx)=True. Inconsistency ... a set of assertions that cannot all simultaneously satisfy a specified logical model. Contradiction is relational. Inconsistency is a property of a set/state.
a_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes Contradiction (a relational property between two specific assertions under a context) from Inconsistency (a property of an entire assertion set/state under a logical model).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Context must be checked first ... Nexus_{Production}=3.70 and Nexus_{Staging}=3.69 ... no contradiction because Context(P_1)\neq Context(P_2). Different context \Rightarrow not necessarily contradictory. Many apparent contradictions are actually missing-dimension problems.
a_rows_sample.statement: Reaffirms that differing contexts (production vs staging) can make apparently conflicting values non-contradictory, restating that many apparent contradictions are missing-dimension problems.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Contradiction requires a conflict rule ... Conflict_\rho(A_i,A_j) = Rule_\rho(P_i,P_j,C_i,C_j) ... Version(x)=v_1 \land Version(x)=v_2 \land v_1\neq v_2 is contradictory if the two assertions refer to the same system; same environment; same temporal scope. Without those conditions: DifferentValues\n
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines Conflict_ρ(A_i,A_j)=Rule_ρ(P_i,P_j,C_i,C_j): contradiction requires an explicit rule checking same system/environment/temporal scope, so DifferentValues ≠ Contradiction without those conditions.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Conflict graph ... a knowledge conflict graph: G_C=(A,L_C) ... A1: Nexus production = 3.69 conflict A2: Nexus production = 3.70. The conflict is explicitly represented. Neither assertion has to be deleted.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines a knowledge conflict graph G_C=(A,L_C) (assertions and conflict relations) representing conflicts explicitly without deleting either assertion.

a_rows_sample.anchor: KnowledgeOS should preserve both assertions ... A_1\in K_t \land A_2\in K_t \land Conflict(A_1,A_2)=Active. This is a legitimate Knowledge State. The state is inconsistent with respect to that proposition, but it is not computationally unusable.
a_rows_sample.statement: States that a Knowledge State holding both A1 and A2 with an Active conflict marker is legitimate and computationally usable, despite being inconsistent with respect to that proposition.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Paraconsistent principle ... P,\neg P \not\Rightarrow Q for arbitrary Q. Contradiction must remain local. ... we do not necessarily need to commit the entire KnowledgeOS kernel to one particular paraconsistent logic ... the kernel must support the invariant: Local inconsistency does not imply global
a_rows_sample.statement: States the paraconsistent principle P,¬P ⇏ Q (contradiction must remain local), without committing the kernel to any specific paraconsistent logic (e.g. Priest's LP), requiring only that local inconsistency not imply global triviality.

a_rows_sample.anchor: A useful four-valued interpretation ... P supported ... \neg P supported ... Unknown ... Supported true-side ... Supported false-side ... Conflicted ... \mathbb B=\{00,10,01,11\} ... This is much more expressive than True/False.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines a four-valued epistemic-status model B={00,10,01,11} (Unknown, P-supported, ¬P-supported, Conflicted) as more expressive than binary True/False.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Important correction ... We should not interpret 10=True and 01=False. They mean: Evidence currently supports one side. This is epistemic status, not metaphysical truth. Four-valued epistemic status\neq Four-valued truth.
a_rows_sample.statement: Corrects a likely misreading of the four-valued model: its values denote epistemic support status, not metaphysical truth values — Four-valued epistemic status ≠ Four-valued truth.

a_rows_sample.anchor: This fits our existing epistemic model ... \Sigma_A=(Acquisition,Support,Uncertainty,Validity) and conflict remains external: C=(A_i,A_j,Rule,Context,Status). \Sigma_A does not need to contain Conflicted because conflict belongs to the relationship between assertions.
a_rows_sample.statement: Confirms conflict is a relational property external to the per-assertion state Σ_A, which need not include a 'Conflicted' field since conflict belongs between assertions, not within one.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Conflict intensity is not a universal scalar ... ConflictScore=0.8 ... I recommend we don't. Instead represent Conflict: Assertions, Rule, Context, EvidenceBasis, Status: Active. Conflict representation is fundamental. Conflict score is derived.
a_rows_sample.statement: Warns against a scalar ConflictScore, preferring a structured conflict record (assertions, rule, context, evidence basis, status): conflict representation is fundamental, any scalar score is derived.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Belief revision ... K_t\models P and new evidence supports \neg P. K_{t+1}=Revise(K_t,e). Revision does not necessarily mean deleting P. retain both and mark conflict; contextualize; downgrade one; retract one; supersede one; accept one and reject the other; leave unresolved. Which occurs depends on
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines the revision operation K_{t+1}=Revise(K_t,e) with seven possible policy-dependent outcomes (retain both with conflict marked, contextualize, downgrade, retract, supersede, accept-one-reject-other, leave unresolved) — none of which is automatic deletion.

a_rows_sample.anchor: AGM-style belief revision is useful—but not sufficient ... revision; contraction; consistency; minimal change. But KnowledgeOS has a different requirement: We may intentionally retain inconsistent information. Therefore classical consistency-preserving belief revision is not sufficient as the sole k
a_rows_sample.statement: Argues classical AGM-style (consistency-preserving) belief revision is insufficient alone, since KnowledgeOS may intentionally retain inconsistent information; needs a more general evidence-based, contradiction-tolerant revision model.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Three different responses to conflict ... A. Contextual resolution ... No real contradiction. B. Epistemic resolution ... one assertion may become Retracted or Rejected. C. Irreducible conflict ... Conflict=Unresolved and KnowledgeOS retains both. This is a perfectly legitimate endpoint.
a_rows_sample.statement: Classifies three conflict responses: Contextual resolution (no real contradiction once context is added), Epistemic resolution (one side retracted/rejected on evidential grounds), and Irreducible conflict (both retained as Unresolved, a legitimate endpoint).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Unresolvable is not failure ... two authoritative sources disagree and there is no way to determine which is correct. KnowledgeOS should be able to say P: Contested rather than inventing P=True. Unresolvable is a valid knowledge state.
a_rows_sample.statement: States Unresolvable is a valid knowledge state: when two authoritative sources irreconcilably disagree, KnowledgeOS should record P:Contested rather than inventing a resolution.

a_rows_sample.anchor: What should Zero do? ... Zero detects Conflict(A_1,A_2). It creates a discrepancy d_{conflict} with involved assertions; conflict rule; context; severity; evidence basis; age; impact. Zero(K,I) \rightarrow \Delta_{conflict}.
a_rows_sample.statement: Extends Zero's role to conflict detection: Zero(K,I)→Δ_conflict, a structured discrepancy record with assertions, rule, context, severity, evidence basis, age, impact.

a_rows_sample.anchor: What should Lord do? ... What information could resolve this conflict? ... Query live API. Inspect deployment manifest. Inspect filesystem. Ask system owner. The candidates are evaluated using Step 6: VOE(q). Conflict \rightarrow Gap \rightarrow CandidateEvidence \rightarrow ExpectedDiscrepancyReduc
a_rows_sample.statement: Extends Lord's role to conflict resolution: proposing candidate evidence acquisitions (query API, inspect manifest/filesystem, ask owner) evaluated via the Step 6 Value-of-Evidence machinery, connecting Conflict→Gap→CandidateEvidence→ExpectedDiscrepancyReduction.

a_rows_sample.anchor: What should Sārathi do? ... severity; purpose; cost; authority; safety; urgency; expected value. It may decide Investigate. Or AcceptRisk. Or Defer. Or CommitWithConflict. A decision does not necessarily require complete epistemic resolution.
a_rows_sample.statement: Extends Sārathi's role to conflict handling with four possible decisions (Investigate/AcceptRisk/Defer/CommitWithConflict), noting a decision does not require complete epistemic resolution.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Example — Architecture decision ... Migration is technically feasible ... Migration introduces unacceptable operational risk ... TechnicalFeasibility=True ... OperationalRisk=High ... the apparent conflict becomes a multi-dimensional decision problem. Conflict detection can reveal a modeling deficie
a_rows_sample.statement: Shows an apparent architecture-decision contradiction (feasible vs unacceptable risk) resolves into a multi-dimensional decision problem once separated into distinct dimensions (TechnicalFeasibility, OperationalRisk) — conflict detection can reveal a modeling deficiency.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Temporal conflict ... Nexus=3.69 at t_1=2024 and Nexus=3.85 at t_2=2026. There is no contradiction if t_1\neq t_2. Temporal context must be part of conflict detection. This is one of the reasons we separated SourceTime, AcquisitionTime, ValidityTime.
a_rows_sample.statement: Requires temporal context be part of conflict detection, since two differently-timed version assertions are not contradictory — reaffirming the earlier SourceTime/AcquisitionTime/ValidityTime separation.

b_rows_sample.anchor: A common mistake is to say A_1,A_2\Rightarrow A_3 therefore A_3 has "the same confidence" as A_1,A_2. That is generally false. The epistemic quality of a derived proposition depends on what kind of inference produced it, what premises it depends on, how those premises depend on one another, and what
b_rows_sample.statement: Warns against assuming a derived proposition inherits its premises' confidence wholesale; its epistemic quality depends on the inference kind, premise dependencies, and the inference rule's own uncertainty.

b_rows_sample.anchor: The fundamental problem ... A_1=Strong and A_2=Weak. A_3=A_1\land A_2 ... It cannot simply inherit Strong. Nor should we arbitrarily assign Weak. ... \Sigma_{derived} = Propagate_\rho(\Sigma_{premises},Rule,Method,Dependency,Context)
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines Σ_derived=Propagate_ρ(Σ_premises,Rule,Method,Dependency,Context) as the general propagation function, illustrated by a conjunction of a Strong and a Weak premise where neither naive inheritance is correct.

b_rows_sample.anchor: First distinction: uncertainty has different origins ... Premise uncertainty U_{premise} ... Inference uncertainty U_{inference} ... Model uncertainty U_{model} ... Measurement uncertainty U_{measurement} ... Semantic uncertainty U_{semantic} ... Context uncertainty U_{context} ... Uncertainty\neq o
b_rows_sample.statement: Enumerates six distinct uncertainty origins — premise, inference, model, measurement, semantic, context — establishing Uncertainty ≠ one universal quantity.

b_rows_sample.anchor: This confirms our multidimensional model ... U_A=(U_{source},U_{measurement},U_{semantic},U_{inference},U_{model},U_{context}) ... more rigorous than U_A=0.3. A scalar may later be derived if a policy needs one.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines a six-dimension uncertainty vector U_A, more rigorous than a bare scalar U_A=0.3, from which a policy-specific scalar may later be derived.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Dependency graph ... G_D=(V,E_D) ... A1, A2 → A3 → A5 ... Deps(A_3)=\{A_1,A_2\} and Deps(A_5)=\{A_3\}. Therefore uncertainty can propagate through the graph.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines a derivation dependency graph G_D=(V,E_D) with Deps(A) giving direct premise sets, through which uncertainty can propagate.

b_rows_sample.anchor: But propagation depends on the inference method ... y=2x ... \sigma_y=2\sigma_x=0.2 ... a mathematical propagation rule. But now consider ... x is probably caused by y ... an abductive inference. Its uncertainty cannot be propagated using the same formula. PropagationFunction depends on InferenceMet
b_rows_sample.statement: Shows via a linear-uncertainty-propagation example (y=2x, σ_y=2σ_x) contrasted with an abductive inference that the propagation function itself depends on the inference method, not a single universal formula.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Deterministic derivation ... A_1\vdash Q ... the derivation itself does not introduce statistical uncertainty. However, the premises may still have epistemic uncertainty. Deterministic rule \not\Rightarrow uncertain premises. The rule may be certain while its inputs are not.
b_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes rule certainty from premise certainty: a deterministic derivation rule does not itself add uncertainty, but its premises may still be epistemically uncertain — Deterministic rule ⇏ uncertain premises.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Statistical inference ... \hat\theta=10.2 with SE(\hat\theta)=0.4. The uncertainty belongs to the statistical inference. KnowledgeOS must preserve Estimate=10.2 and Uncertainty=0.4 rather than reducing the output to 10.2.
b_rows_sample.statement: Requires KnowledgeOS to preserve a statistical estimate together with its standard error (e.g. 10.2 ± 0.4) rather than collapsing to the point estimate alone.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Correlated evidence ... E_2=Copy(E_1), then Information(E_2\mid E_1)\approx0. Dependency structure must participate in uncertainty/support propagation.
b_rows_sample.statement: Restates that strongly correlated/copied evidence adds near-zero additional information, so dependency structure must participate in uncertainty/support propagation, not be treated as independent.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Unknown dependency ... a conservative policy might produce Support_{combined}\leq Support_{assuming independence}. But that inequality is policy-dependent, not a universal mathematical theorem. The kernel should preserve Dependency=Unknown. The assessment calculus decides what to do.
b_rows_sample.statement: Notes a conservative policy may cap combined support below the independence assumption when dependency is unknown, but this inequality is policy-dependent, not a universal theorem — the kernel only preserves Dependency=Unknown.

b_rows_sample.anchor: The most important statistical distinction ... P(A)=0.9 and P(B)=0.9 ... If independent P(A\land B)=0.81. If perfectly dependent P(A\land B)=0.9. Marginal confidence does not determine joint confidence. This is a major reason KnowledgeOS cannot use naive confidence multiplication.
b_rows_sample.statement: Uses two 0.9-confidence propositions to show joint confidence ranges from 0.81 (independent) to 0.9 (perfectly dependent) — marginal confidence does not determine joint confidence, ruling out naive confidence multiplication.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Statistical propagation needs a model ... Y=f(X_1,\ldots,X_n) ... Var(Y)\approx J\Sigma_XJ^T ... Covariance matters. This maps beautifully to our evidence-dependency model.
b_rows_sample.statement: Notes formal statistical uncertainty propagation Var(Y)≈JΣ_XJ^T requires the full covariance matrix, mapping naturally onto the evidence-dependency model — covariance matters, not just marginal uncertainties.

b_rows_sample.anchor: KnowledgeOS should therefore preserve dependency, not just scores ... A1 confidence = 0.9, A2 confidence = 0.9 ... instead A1, A2, Dependency(A1,A2) = Independent / Dependent / Unknown. Then a calculus can determine the appropriate combination. This is one of the strongest architectural consequences
b_rows_sample.statement: Argues KnowledgeOS must store per-pair Dependency status alongside confidence scores rather than bare scores alone, called one of the strongest architectural consequences of the theory.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Derived knowledge should retain its dependency graph ... A_3=f(A_1,A_2). Basis(A_3)=\{A_1,A_2\}. If A_1 is retracted, we do not automatically retract A_3. Instead Reassess(A_3). This follows directly from Step 9.
b_rows_sample.statement: Requires derived assertions retain their basis (Basis(A3)={A1,A2}), so retracting one premise triggers Reassess, not automatic retraction — following directly from Step 9's dependency-propagation invariant.

b_rows_sample.statement: Traces the AcceptancePolicy (the object whose mis-layering caused the most recorded trouble in the programme) through all five layers as a worked example: as content it is L2 material at rest in K_t; as the governor of admission it is an L2 object with an L1 shadow (Article 3 forbids self-authorization, I-11 forbids ungoverned change); any enforcement would be L4 code that must first consult the governance record; and the failure the layering prevents is the programme's most-sighted defect (the policy that governs while nothing governs it, sighted independently four times, per Chapter III.8).

b_rows_sample.anchor: FOUR interlocking guards make the modification governed rather than wild: 1. Mode separation... 2. The change is a Decision under contract... 3. Versioning with a transition schema... 4. Recursive self-subjection... The governor is inside the governed store, not above it.
b_rows_sample.statement: States the chapter's central answer to why self-modifying admission policy is not an uncontrolled system: four interlocking guards -- (1) mode separation (proposed policy is content only, force requires the approved in-force version; "a rule that is sort of in effect" is unrepresentable), (2) the change is a Decision under the full III.7 Decision-Contract machinery (no-averaging conjunction, Unknown->Block, Auth as an act, per A6), (3) versioning with a transition schema (change rationale, authority, effective date, superseded version, verification; forward-only supersession), and (4) recursive self-subjection (Constitution subset-of AuthoritativeKnowledge -- the governing documents obey their own provenance/authority/temporal-validity/traceability disciplines) -- making self-modification exist exactly once, as a narrow contract-guarded versioned human-authorized transition, with every other path a type error.

a_rows_sample.anchor: I attacked my own proposal. Ten attacks, executed. 7 survived, 3 refuted.
a_rows_sample.statement: Runs 10 executed adversarial attacks against the candidate knowledge-state tuple K={(q,s,e,c,t,u)}; 7 survive: expressing Unknown (s=Unknown,e=empty,u=unknown, distinct from Refuted), expressing contradiction as a computable relation over two items (not a state property), distinguishing missingness-from-K from present-with-Unknown, provenance without circularity (evidence field e holds opaque evidence-reference ids, not evidence objects, so K need not contain E and E need not contain K), a base case K0 with zero transformations existing (breaking the assumed K->T->K cycle dependency), decidable structural equality (frozenset of frozen records), and supersession via closing t.valid_to plus adding a successor (no extra field needed, bitemporality suffices).

a_rows_sample.anchor: R1 -- non-identifiability is NOT a field... R2 -- structural equality is insufficient... R3 -- the status type is mine, not the corpus's.
a_rows_sample.statement: Three of the ten attacks refute the original proposal: R1, non-identifiability must be a relation over (K1,K2,H,Q) -- two states observationally equivalent under an observation map -- not a label-valued attribute of one item; R2, structural equality is insufficient, shown by an executed counterexample where identical knowledge re-ingested under a new evidence id (E-001 -> E-001-dup) is structurally unequal, so equality must be a FAMILY of relations, not one; R3, the STATUS_VOCAB type is the verifier's own invention -- the corpus has eleven competing vocabularies and designates none, so status is UNDERDETERMINED BY CORPUS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Item = (q: Prop, s: Status, e: FrozenSet[EvidenceRef], c: Context, t: Interval(...), u: Unc) ... eq_struct, eq_sem, eq_obs ... nonidentifiable(K1,K2,H,Q) ... G(input,K,ctx,auth,pol) in {0,1}
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines a repaired, fully executable knowledge-state kernel: Item=(q,s,e,c,t,u) with K=FrozenSet[Item]; an equality FAMILY of three distinct relations (eq_struct: literal equality; eq_sem: equality ignoring evidence ids/uncertainty width; eq_obs: equality relative to an explicit observation map H); non-identifiability as the relation H(K1)=H(K2) AND Q(K1)!=Q(K2); and a total, decidable governance predicate G(input,K,ctx,auth,pol) in {0,1}. Every symbol has an explicit value -- no placeholders or oracles.

a_rows_sample.statement: Executes and reports verbatim a concrete state transition: K0 contains one Supported item (Nexus version 3.69); an Add of version 3.70 with new evidence, under policy P-infra-v1 and architect authority in context infra, is admissible (G=1); K1 results with two items (3.69 superseded, valid_to closed; 3.70 added) plus a generated provenance record; the three equality relations disagree on the pair (structural=False, semantic=False, observational=True) and nonidentifiable(K0,K1,H,Q)=True (H cannot distinguish them, Q can). a_rows_sample.anchor: T1,T2 in T_G does not necessarily imply T2 o T1 in T_G. The audit correctly identifies this as a closure failure. Therefore we must distinguish T from T_G. ... 'transformation algebra' = working name, not established mathematical classification.
a_rows_sample.statement: Corrects the assumption of a closed 'transformation algebra': the corpus's own Step-232 audit shows the governed transformation set T_G is not closed under composition (T1,T2 in T_G does not imply T2 o T1 in T_G), so the unrestricted collection T must be distinguished from the actually-governed T_G, and 'transformation algebra' is downgraded to a working name rather than an established classification.

a_rows_sample.anchor: K_{t+1} = T_t(K_t) subject to G(T_t,C_t,A_t,P_t)=1 and E_t |= Req(T_t,P_t). The audit identifies this as the best-formed transition rule in the corpus. ... the latter is not yet executable, because |= and Req remain undefined.
a_rows_sample.statement: Adopts the corpus's best-formed transition rule K_{t+1}=T_t(K_t) subject to governance admissibility G(T,C,A,P)=1 and an evidence-satisfaction requirement E|=Req(T,P), separating state transition, governance admissibility, and evidence admissibility as three distinct functions -- while noting the evidence-satisfaction relation |= and the requirement function Req remain formally undefined and the rule is therefore not yet executable.

a_rows_sample.anchor: T(K) is not equivalent to Allowed(T,K). Instead Allowed(T,K,C,A,P,E) must be evaluated first. Then, if allowed: T(K,theta)=K'. ... This is directly supported by the corpus's separation of transition from permission to transition.
a_rows_sample.statement: Establishes the architectural separation between a transformation's effect T(K) and its permissibility Allowed(T,K,C,A,P,E), proposing a pipeline (K,T,C,A,P,E) -> Admissible? -> K'=T(K,theta), grounded in the corpus's own separation of transition from permission to transition.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 10 operations classified: Transform (State transition, CORPUS ESTABLISHES); Validate (Assessment, CORPUS ESTABLISHES); Add (Partial state operation, CORPUS ESTABLISHES); Revise (PARTIALLY VERIFIED); Merge/Supersede/Split/Remove/Reject/Replay (OPEN).
a_rows_sample.statement: Classifies 10 mandate-required operations against the Step-232 audit: Transform, Validate and Add are corpus-established (with distinct roles: state transition, assessment, and explicitly partial operation respectively); Revise is only partially verified; Merge, Supersede, Split, Remove, Reject and Replay are all OPEN -- explicitly matching the detailed Step-232 audit rather than the earlier assumption that every operation belongs to one algebra.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Add_x(K) a partial operation. ... Add: K x X -harpoonup-> K. ... Add(K,x) may be undefined when x violates an invariant. Thus Pre_Add(K,x) must hold before the operation is defined.
a_rows_sample.statement: Preserves Add as an explicitly partial operation (K x X -harpoonup-> K, undefined when x violates an invariant, requiring a precondition Pre_Add(K,x)), preferring this over the mathematically dishonest alternative of treating Add as total.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Revise involves new state + historical relation. ... revision appears to involve two outputs: (K',r) where r in HistoryRelation. ... because the corpus does not explicitly type the historical relation, we must keep this PROPOSED rather than promoted.
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes that Revise may actually produce two outputs -- the revised state K' and a historical relation r in HistoryRelation -- since the historical fact K leadsto K' is not necessarily part of K' itself, but keeps this candidate signature (K x X x X' -harpoonup-> K x HistoryRelation) explicitly PROPOSED, not promoted, since the corpus never types HistoryRelation.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Validate: K x X -> Assessment. Validation may subsequently trigger a state transition. Therefore Validate != Transform. This is CORPUS ESTABLISHES. ... Validation -> Assessment while Decision -> Transformation is a candidate architecture. The exact Decision signature remains unresolved.
a_rows_sample.statement: Confirms as corpus-established that Validate (K x X -> Assessment) is categorically different from Transform, and that validation is not necessarily mutating -- a later Decision function (unresolved signature) may map an Assessment to a specific transformation T_d, giving the candidate two-stage architecture Validation->Assessment, Decision->Transformation.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The corpus explicitly rejects Merge(K1,K2)=K1 union K2 as a sufficient definition: Merge != SetUnion. ... A merge must presumably determine: conflicting assertions; identity; provenance; temporal validity; epistemic status; duplicate objects; resulting invariants. But these are requirements to inves
a_rows_sample.statement: Records the corpus's explicit rejection of a naive set-union definition of Merge, listing 7 open requirements a real merge operation must resolve (conflicting assertions, identity, provenance, temporal validity, epistemic status, duplicate objects, resulting invariants) while explicitly refusing to invent a signature for any of them.

a_rows_sample.anchor: To determine whether one state supersedes another, we need some notion of K1 = K2 or at least identity of the relevant knowledge object. Since knowledge-state equality remains undefined, the operation cannot yet be formally closed. Supersede = OPEN and the blocker is: Equality.
a_rows_sample.statement: Identifies undefined Knowledge-State equality as the specific and sole blocker preventing Supersede from being formally closed -- a precise, load-bearing dependency rather than a vague open item.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The key question is whether removing an object means: deleting it; marking it invalid; superseding it; retracting its epistemic status; removing it from a projection while preserving provenance. These are mathematically different operations. Remove = UNDEFINED at signature level. ... Reject listed b
a_rows_sample.statement: Records Remove as undefined even at the signature level, since 'removing' could mean 5 mathematically distinct operations (deletion, invalidity marking, supersession, epistemic-status retraction, or projection-removal preserving provenance); records Reject as effectively abandoned in the audited corpus (OPEN); and records Replay as equality-dependent, since whether replay must reproduce K_n exactly or merely observationally returns to the still-open equality question.

a_rows_sample.anchor: the 'operation set' contains several different kinds of arrows: State transformations (K -harpoonup-> K)... Assessments (K x X -> Assessment)... Historical reconstruction (History x K0 -> K)... Governance predicates (T x C x A x P -> {0,1}). This is a typed family of operations, not yet one algebra.
a_rows_sample.statement: Reconstructs the operation set as a typed family of 4 categorically distinct kinds of arrows (state transformations, assessments, historical reconstruction, governance predicates) rather than one homogeneous algebra of K x X -> K operations -- a substantially stronger and more disciplined result than forcing every operation into one signature shape.

a_rows_sample.anchor: T2 o T1 in T_G iff the composed transformation satisfies the governance constraints. But even that needs a formal definition of G. ... Governance closure = structurally described, computationally unresolved.
a_rows_sample.statement: States the correct (conditional, not universal) closure criterion for composed transformations under governance: T2 o T1 is in T_G if and only if the composed transformation itself satisfies the governance constraints -- but notes this criterion cannot yet be evaluated since G's algorithm, though well-typed (G(T,K,C,A,P) in {0,1}), is absent; governance closure is structurally described but computationally unresolved.

a_rows_sample.anchor: We should now reject the simplistic architecture: T = one closed algebra of state transformations. ... KnowledgeOS transformation system containing: state transitions, assessments, governance predicates, historical reconstruction, possibly decisions/events, with typed connections between them. Wheth
a_rows_sample.statement: States the step's central architectural conclusion, rejecting the simplistic 'one closed algebra' hypothesis in favor of a typed KnowledgeOS transformation system (state transitions, assessments, governance predicates, historical reconstruction, possibly decisions/events, all typed-connected), while explicitly leaving open whether this deserves the mathematical name category, partial algebra, transition system, or something else, per the governing mandate's instruction not to prematurely choose a structure.

a_rows_sample.anchor: State represents domain knowledge. Assessment represents an evaluation of knowledge. Decision potentially represents a governed choice. Transformation changes domain state. Governance determines whether the transformation is admissible. History preserves/reconstructs evolution. These should therefor
a_rows_sample.statement: Maps the mathematical typed-arrow separation directly onto a DDD boundary test: State, Assessment, Decision, Transformation, Governance and History are 6 distinct domain roles that should not automatically collapse into a single Aggregate, entity, or service, citing the corpus's own warning against conflating bounded contexts, aggregates, database tables and domain events.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The hypothesis that KnowledgeOS has one closed transformation algebra over K is now weakened. ... KnowledgeOS has a typed transformation/assessment/governance system. ... The correct mathematical structure remains UNRESOLVED until equality, domains, composition and closure are fully specified.
a_rows_sample.statement: Concludes Step 249 by weakening the one-closed-algebra hypothesis to a typed transformation/assessment/governance system, explicitly leaving the correct final mathematical structure UNRESOLVED pending full specification of equality, domains, composition and closure -- and sets Step 250 (Knowledge-State Equality and Identity Gate) as the next mandatory test, since undefined equality is identified as blocking Merge, Supersede and Replay specifically.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Validate: K x X -> Assessment. ... validation may subsequently trigger a state transition. Therefore Validate not-in T_K ... Instead Validate in A where A = {K x X -> Assessment}. This is one of the strongest findings in Step 250.
a_rows_sample.statement: Reaffirms Validate as the strongest-evidenced operation, explicitly excluded from the state-transformation family T_K and placed instead in the assessment family A={K x X -> Assessment} -- reiterated as one of the step's strongest findings, consistent with S1613's identical conclusion.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Revise = partial state transition with historical consequence is the strongest current characterization. ... signature refinement still OPEN [Revise: K x X x X' -harpoonup-> K x HistoryRelation, unpromoted since HistoryRelation is untyped].
a_rows_sample.statement: Reaffirms Revise's characterization from Step 249: corpus-established as a partial state-changing operation with a historical consequence, but its exact richer signature (producing a typed HistoryRelation alongside the new state) remains open since HistoryRelation itself is untyped.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The corpus defines Remove_x: K -harpoonup-> K. The operation is explicitly partial because removing one item may invalidate dependent knowledge. This means Remove in T_K is currently defensible. And Remove is partial. This is a stronger result than we had at Step 249.
a_rows_sample.statement: Reclassifies Remove as CORPUS-ESTABLISHES (a partial operation Remove_x:K-harpoonup->K, since removing one item may invalidate dependent knowledge) -- the file explicitly calls this 'a stronger result than we had at Step 249', where the same operation was instead rated UNDEFINED at signature level (S1613); the two adjacent same-day step files disagree on Remove's status without either citing the other's specific verdict.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Add_x: K -harpoonup-> K is the mathematically safer formulation. The corpus explicitly calls it a partial operation. ... Supersede: at minimum, supersession requires identifying what is being superseded. That immediately creates an equality/identity dependency ... Supersede = UNRESOLVED with blocker
a_rows_sample.statement: Reaffirms Add as a corpus-established partial operation (constrained by Invariant(K')=True), and reaffirms Supersede as UNRESOLVED, naming its blockers precisely as Equality, Identity, and TemporalSemantics -- consistent with and sharpening S1613's identification of equality as Supersede's blocker.

a_rows_sample.anchor: S = (K, T, A, Q, E, H, D, G) [Knowledge states, State transformations T:KxI-harpoonup->K, Assessments A:KxX->Assessment, Queries Q:KxI->Result, Events E, History H, Decisions D, Governance G:TxCxAxP->{0,1}]. This is not yet the final KnowledgeOS mathematical structure. It is the smallest currently d
a_rows_sample.statement: Assembles the strongest current typed-family structure S=(K,T,A,Q,E,H,D,G) with 8 named components (knowledge states, partial state transformations, assessments, queries, events, history, decisions, governance predicates) -- explicitly not the final structure, but the smallest currently defensible typed candidate family, extending S1613's 4-arrow-kind classification with Queries and Decisions made explicit.

b_rows_sample.anchor: We must not force every operation into T:K->K because Step 255 already demonstrated that some operations may depend on external policy, authority, time, evidence or other typed context.
b_rows_sample.statement: Applies Step 255's finding directly: no operation should be forced into the shape T:K->K, since operations may legitimately depend on external typed context (policy, authority, time, evidence) rather than K alone.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Add requires a definition of identity/equality. This directly links Step 256 back to the unresolved Equality_K. ... set-like semantics Add(K,x)=K union {x} [versus] identity-aware semantics [which] may reject an object whose identity already exists.
b_rows_sample.statement: Shows Add cannot be formally defined until equality/identity is resolved, since two radically different semantics remain open: plain set-union (duplicates silently absorbed) versus identity-aware rejection of objects whose identity already exists.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Does removal mean x not-in K' or x in K' with status Withdrawn? These are radically different semantics. ... Remove != Withdraw unless the vocabulary explicitly decides otherwise. ... Reject(x) != Remove(x). This is an important Ubiquitous Language distinction.
b_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes true deletion from lifecycle-status change as radically different operation semantics, concluding Remove != Withdraw and Reject != Remove unless the theory explicitly decides to identify them -- since a status-changed object remains represented in K while a deleted one does not.

b_rows_sample.anchor: revision requires identity preservation: id(x')=id(x)? If yes, Revision(x,x') is a state transition on one entity. If no, Revision is actually Remove(x)+Add(x'). ... What makes two knowledge objects 'the same object' across revision? ... This is another reason why equality and identity cannot be pos
b_rows_sample.statement: Shows Revise cannot be formally defined until cross-time object identity is resolved: if id(x')=id(x), Revise is a genuine state transition on one entity; if not, Revise reduces to Remove+Add of two different entities -- the same identity/equality dependency recurring across multiple operations.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Provenance(x3) = {Provenance(x1), Provenance(x2)}. If so, Merge is inherently provenance-preserving. This means that the operation registry itself can reveal whether provenance is operationally essential. ... Split requires a preservation invariant.
b_rows_sample.statement: Shows Merge is diagnostically important for the provenance question: if the merged object's provenance is the union of its sources' provenances, Merge is inherently provenance-preserving, meaning the operation registry itself (not abstract argument) can reveal whether provenance is operationally essential; separately notes Split requires an explicit semantic-preservation invariant across its decomposition.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Every semantically relevant external variable must be explicit. ... T: K x Policy x Time -> K'. This is preferable to hiding Policy or Time inside an implicit global context. ... Deterministic Transformation != Immutable Knowledge.
b_rows_sample.statement: States a determinism-discipline principle: any externally-varying quantity a transformation depends on (e.g. current time, applicable policy) must be an explicit function argument, never an implicit global, or the transformation appears nondeterministic to the mathematical model; separately clarifies determinism (same inputs, same result) is orthogonal to immutability of the overall knowledge base.

b_rows_sample.anchor: R(T_i) = (Name, Domain, Codomain, Preconditions, Postconditions, Invariants, Parameters, Dependencies, Determinism, ProvenanceDependency, HistoryDependency, PolicyDependency, IdentityDependency) becomes the working registry schema.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines the working operation-registry schema R(T_i) with 13 fields, extending the mandate's original 9-field proposal with explicit PolicyDependency and IdentityDependency flags.

b_rows_sample.anchor: we should not assume closure: T_i,T_j in T => T_j o T_i in T. The earlier audit already found that the governed transformation subset is not demonstrated closed under composition.
b_rows_sample.statement: Reaffirms the corpus's established finding that the governed transformation subset is not closed under composition, applying it to the operation-registry construction: composition T_j o T_i is only meaningful when Codomain(T_i) intersects Domain(T_j), and closure must never be assumed.

b_rows_sample.anchor: T_Add: K x X -> K, T_Merge: K x X x X -> K, Validate: K x E -> Result, Approve: Candidate x Authority -> ApprovedCandidate. Therefore KnowledgeOS may be better modeled as a typed transition system than as a single algebra.
b_rows_sample.statement: Confirms operations need not share one homogeneous signature shape by giving 4 explicitly differently-typed example operations, reaffirming the typed-transition-system (not single algebra) conclusion already reached in Steps 249-250.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Validate not-equiv Transform. This prevents a common category error in the kernel. ... Command is not Transformation ... Command -> Decision -> Transformation -> NewState ... Event != T. The corpus already distinguishes Command -> Transformation -> Event.
b_rows_sample.statement: Reaffirms three category-error-preventing non-collapses for the operation vocabulary: Validate != Transform (validation may determine valid/invalid without changing K); Command != Transformation (command is intent/request, not the state change itself); Event != Transformation (an event records an occurrence, distinct from the state-evolution-defining function).

b_rows_sample.anchor: ProvDep(T_i) in {0,1,?} ... This gives us a way to empirically determine where history must survive. ... transforms the vague question 'Does provenance belong in K?' into the operational question: exists T in T: ProvDep(T)=1? If yes, then provenance-sensitive information must be available to that op
b_rows_sample.statement: Converts the recurring vague 'does provenance belong in K' question into a precise operational test using explicit per-operation dependency flags (ProvDep, HistDep, PolicyDep in {0,1,?}): if any operation has ProvDep=1, provenance-sensitive information must be accessible to it, and only then does the placement question (K-resident, T-parameter, or external context) arise -- directly implementing S1621's Type-I/II/III taxonomy as a concrete research tool.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Required(T) = StateReq(T) union ContextReq(T). Only StateReq(T) constrains K. ... K* = argmin_K Complexity(K) subject to semantic sufficiency.
b_rows_sample.statement: Refines the kernel-minimization target by splitting an operation's total required information into StateReq(T) (must be resident in K) and ContextReq(T) (may be supplied externally, does not constrain K), restating the optimization target K*=argmin Complexity(K) subject to semantic sufficiency with this refined split.

b_rows_sample.anchor: T must be typed before K can be minimized. Operations may be partial. Operations need not share one homogeneous signature. Validation, Command, Event and Transformation must not be conflated. Provenance/History/Policy dependence must be explicitly tested per operation. Not established: the nine cand
b_rows_sample.statement: Consolidates the step's established-versus-not-established results: established that T must be typed before K can be minimized, operations may be partial, need not share one signature, and 4 key terms must not be conflated, with dependency-testing mandatory per operation; explicitly not established that the 9 candidate operations or any particular signature is final.

b_rows_sample.anchor: The most important unresolved signatures are: Supersede, Merge, Revise, Transform. These operations have the highest potential to distinguish competing state/history models. ... Step 257 -- Formalize the Four Discriminating Operations ... Then we can run the first real congruence experiment ... That
b_rows_sample.statement: Names Supersede, Merge, Revise and Transform as the 4 highest-value operations for distinguishing competing state/history models, and sets Step 257 as their complete formalization (across domain/codomain/preconditions/postconditions/identity/provenance/history/policy/determinism/composability) in order to run the first real congruence experiment -- explicitly judged stronger evidence than proposing yet another candidate kernel tuple.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 12 operations fully specified [create, assert, retract, relate, merge, supersede, refine, resolve, remove, replay, validate, assess] each with Input/Preconditions/Output/Postconditions/Det/Auth/Gov/Hist/Computable/Failure modes. All 12 rated Computable=YES.
b_rows_sample.statement: Fully specifies concrete 11-field signatures for 12 named operations (create, assert, retract, relate, merge, supersede, refine, resolve, remove, replay, validate, assess), each rated computable=YES, directly executing the operation-registry schema Step 256 (S1623) had proposed abstractly -- e.g. retract has failure mode LOSSY-NO-INVERSE (executed), relate can fail via a cycle, merge may introduce contradiction (executed), replay is order-dependent (executed).

b_rows_sample.anchor: T: K x Q x C -> K' [not necessarily unary]. It simply means that transformation is a typed state transition, not necessarily a closed unary function. ... hidden inputs are forbidden ... Every semantically relevant external dependency must be explicit. ... Prov(k') = Prov(k) union Prov(q) union Prov(
b_rows_sample.statement: Confirms Transform need not be unary (T:KxQxC->K', a typed state transition rather than a closed K->K function), reaffirms that every semantically relevant external dependency (policy, time, authority, evidence) must be an explicit argument to preserve determinism, and proposes an unestablished provenance-propagation model Prov(k')=Prov(k) union Prov(q) union Prov(c) for Transform specifically.

group_evidence.why_grouped: explicit agent-stated uncertainty: 's1623-operation-registry-schema-and-dependency-matrix' POSSIBLY relates to 's1613-transformation-system-typed-graph-not-algebra' (batch B0039). Note: Step 256's 13-field operation-registry schema and 9x6 operation-to-information dependency matrix, converting the vague provenance-placement question into a precise per-operation test (ProvDep(T)=1?); shows Add/Revise cannot be defined until identity/equality is resolved and Merge is diagnostic for provenance necessity; names Supersede/Merge/Revise/Transform as the four highest-value discriminating operations, formalized next in Step 257.

a_rows_sample.anchor: docs/knowledge/ is the Engineering Knowledge Platform (EKP): a governed, linted, deterministic knowledge graph with unique ids, typed relations, cycle detection, and controlled vocabularies for authority and lifecycle. It runs. I executed it. ... 250 steps of formal theory were written beside a work
a_rows_sample.statement: Discovers via a 1467-file corpus scan that docs/knowledge/ (the Engineering Knowledge Platform, EKP) is a running, executed, governed and linted implementation of much of the theory, yet of 311 numbered-step files across 250 distinct step numbers, exactly one (step 153) mentions it, and only via one word ('knowledge-graph'); 21-23 non-step files do reference it -- an independently discovered second instance of the Q7 assertion-layer loss pattern (S1605), now confirmed by scanning implementation references rather than theory content.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 31 distinct definitional statements yield six mutually incompatible types [composed local contracts (071); f(Irreversibility,Impact,Criticality) (092); Strong BC Candidate (127); BackwardTraceability (170); DeterministicAssurance (230, self-referential); a boolean]. Step 230's self-definition direct
a_rows_sample.statement: Finds 'Assurance' irreparably overloaded across 31 definitional statements collapsing into 6 mutually incompatible types (composed local contracts, a function of irreversibility/impact/criticality, a 'Strong BC Candidate' label, BackwardTraceability, a self-referential DeterministicAssurance, and a plain boolean); Step 230's self-referential definition directly contradicts the corpus's own imported Williamson result that assurance cannot recursively certify itself; and by the corpus's own most-repeated epistemological claim (assurance is strong only where executable, weak where prose), the corpus's own assurance concept is weak -- named completion blocker CB-1, a hard blocker on formal closure.

a_rows_sample.anchor: (K, Merge, empty) is a commutative idempotent monoid -- a JOIN-SEMILATTICE. Executed. ... Contradict is symmetric, irreflexive, and NOT transitive -- a tolerance relation, never an equivalence. Any construction treating contradiction as an equivalence class is wrong. ... Remove has no total inverse
a_rows_sample.statement: Extends S1612's proven results with 5 further executed algebraic facts: (K,Merge,empty-set) forms a commutative idempotent monoid, i.e. a join-semilattice; Contradict is symmetric and irreflexive but NOT transitive, making it a tolerance relation rather than an equivalence (any equivalence-class-based construction on contradiction is wrong); Remove has no total inverse (cascading removal loses relations R, non-cascading breaks Valid); Split is lossy on R; and Merge preserves structural validity but not consistency, demonstrated by an executed counterexample where two individually consistent states merge into a contradictory one.

a_rows_sample.anchor: knowledge-lint.php: 37 governed documents, all pass, exit 0. knowledge-graph.php x2: 39 nodes, 70 edges, byte-identical across runs -- DETERMINISTIC. php artisan test --filter=Lineage: 47 passed/125 assertions. --filter=KnowledgeOs: 10 passed/34 assertions. Reference model, 14 probes: 13/14 pass; th
a_rows_sample.statement: Reports 5 executed empirical probes against real systems this session: knowledge-lint.php passes on all 37 governed documents (exit 0); knowledge-graph.php run twice produces byte-identical 39-node/70-edge output (deterministic); php artisan test filters confirm 47/125 (Lineage) and 10/34 (KnowledgeOs) assertions passing, corroborating the '47 tests passing' figure independently found elsewhere in this batch (S1595, S1600); and a 14-probe reference model run passes 13/14, with the one failure diagnosed as genuine theory content (Section 8).

a_rows_sample.anchor: ReplayAssertion -- identity is a content hash including time; policy captured externally as a hash; no status field; documented invariant 'once created is immutable... they do NOT mutate.' EvidenceSet -- 'References are opaque strings... this VO holds no transport' (ADR-T16). Evidence by reference,
a_rows_sample.statement: Finds 4 independent corroborations from unrelated production bounded contexts (convergent evolution, not KnowledgeOS-derived): ReplayAssertion uses a content hash (including time) as identity, captures policy externally, has no status field, and is documented immutable -- matching the S1595 identity-repair direction; EvidenceSet holds evidence strictly by reference, never by value (ADR-T16), exactly matching the corpus derivation's rejection of embedding evidence objects; EventProvenance uses (correlationId,causationId), explicitly scoped to Integration Events only; and authorities.yaml documents governance status as independent of lifecycle status, meaning Sigma-perp-Gamma orthogonality (S1606) is enforced in running production configuration by a linter, not merely a theoretical derivation.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The mandate's chain places Sigma between Assertion and K. That link does not exist. Sigma is not a component of K -- it is derived by Assessment and lives outside. Sigma never gated K. ... Circularity: NONE in the definitional order.
a_rows_sample.statement: Corrects an assumed dependency-chain link: Sigma is not upstream-gating K as an earlier mandate's diagram implied, but is a sibling derived quantity from Assessment, living entirely outside K; confirms no circularity exists in the definitional order overall (Valid is structural and does not invoke Contradict; identity is content-addressed from assertion fields only).

a_rows_sample.anchor: the removal tests justify id and t by appeal to supersession and replay -- operations that are downstream of K. These are requirements, not definitions, and requirements legitimately flow backward. But ... this is the one place where downstream material informs an upstream definition, and the reader
a_rows_sample.statement: Discloses a methodological caveat rather than hiding it: the minimality removal-tests (S1612) justify id and t fields by appeal to supersession and replay, operations downstream of K itself; while requirements legitimately flow backward from operations to definitions, this is flagged as the one place in the derivation where downstream material informs an upstream definition, to be weighed accordingly by readers.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Evidence: OVERLOADED, reference vs object, resolved to reference. Context: assertion-scope vs governance-context, two meanings. Authority: OVERLOADED, actor vs trust-rank. Provenance: THREE OBJECTS, ONE WORD. Validation: vs validity vs verification, three words unclear boundaries. Validity: five sub
a_rows_sample.statement: Runs a corpus-wide (1467-file) ubiquitous-language census with file/step counts per term, confirming and quantifying several terms flagged elsewhere as overloaded (Evidence: reference-vs-object; Context: two meanings; Authority: actor-vs-trust-rank; Provenance: three distinct objects under one word; Validation/Validity/Verification: three words with unclear boundaries; Validity: five sub-predicates), and identifying two corpus concepts (Missingness, Non-identifiability) as effectively abandoned/dead after specific step numbers rather than reconciled.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The three-way provenance collision -- one word, three distinct objects: Pi (an assertion's origin, field of Assertion, Q7); History(T) (the state's transformation record, K->Histories, GovernanceLineageGraph); EventProvenance (a message causal chain, correlationId/causationId, production, Integratio
a_rows_sample.statement: Resolves the open Provenance/Lineage distinction (S1600, S1616) into a definitive three-way finding: Pi (an assertion's own origin, per Q7), History(T) (the state's transformation record, as implemented in GovernanceLineageGraph), and EventProvenance (a message causal chain, correlationId/causationId, used only for Integration Events in production) are three genuinely distinct objects sharing one overloaded word -- the verification programme itself had conflated the first two prior to this phase, and the third (EventProvenance) had been entirely invisible to the corpus.

a_rows_sample.anchor: supersedes exists simultaneously as a relation and a status -- in production. statuses.yaml has superseded (order 7, settled) AND knowledge-relationships.yaml has supersedes/superseded_by with an explicit inverse. b_rows_sample.statement: States the closing theorem G5: Guidance (Zero/Lord/Sarathi) is not a prerequisite for every Knowledge-State transition -- a raw external observation event or a scheduled validity check can trigger delta(K_t,e_t) directly, so the lenses must never be modelled as mandatory middleware sitting between every event and the transition function; renames the pipeline from 'Epistemic Cycle' to 'Epistemic Guidance-and-Transition Cycle' to reflect this.

b_rows_sample.anchor: I strongly recommend introducing: I-hat_t = Candidate Ideal State and I_t = Approved Ideal State ... KnowledgeOS -> I-hat_{t+1} (proposal); Authorize(I-hat_{t+1}) -> I_{t+1}.
b_rows_sample.statement: Introduces a Candidate Ideal State (I-hat) vs Approved Ideal State (I) split mirroring the Q17 recommendation/authorization boundary: KnowledgeOS may only ever produce a candidate revision proposal, and only an explicit Authorize step (by the Knower/governance authority under applicable norms) produces the actually approved I_{t+1}; KnowledgeOS != I_{t+1} but KnowledgeOS -> I-hat_{t+1}.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Sārathi \rightarrow DecisionPosture
b_rows_sample.statement: Corrects Sarathi's output from a binary Stop/Continue decision to a richer DecisionPosture ∈ {Proceed, Investigate, ProceedWithCaveats, Defer, Escalate, UnableToDecide}, argued to be closer to Sarathi's actual role.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Recommendation \neq Assertion
b_rows_sample.statement: Strict boundary: Recommendation ≠ Assertion, Recommendation ≠ Fact, Recommendation ≠ Decision. Sārathi may say 'Investigate the moral obligation dimension' but KnowledgeOS must not silently convert that into 'Therefore Arjuna should fight' — the Knower remains the decision authority unless the domain explicitly delegates that authority. Marked as extremely important for the DDD model.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Candidate \neq Knowledge
b_rows_sample.statement: Lord needs a stronger boundary too: Candidate ≠ Knowledge, Candidate ≠ Evidence, Candidate ≠ Assertion. A presentation should visually distinguish KNOWN / INFERRED / UNKNOWN / CANDIDATE / RECOMMENDED to prevent semantic contamination.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Zero(S_t) \rightarrow EpistemicFindings
b_rows_sample.statement: Reaffirms Zero's role as boundary-finder, not belief-decider: Zero(S_t) -> EpistemicFindings, Presentation ⊇ DecisionRelevant(EpistemicFindings); 'Zero does not decide what the Knower should believe. Zero says: Here is where the state has a boundary.' Also strengthens provenance: EveryDecisionRelevantClaim -> Provenance, with a worked claim-level provenance record example (Acquisition/Evidence/Observed-at/Validity/Conflict/Source).

b_rows_sample.anchor:
Unknown 
eq Absent 
eq NotApplicable 
eq NotObserved 
eq NotYetInvestigated
b_rows_sample.statement: Elevates 'unknown' to a fundamental principle already implicit in Zero: Unknown ≠ Absent ≠ NotApplicable ≠ NotObserved ≠ NotYetInvestigated, illustrated by Version=UNKNOWN not meaning Version=ABSENT, and SecurityStatus=NOT_ASSESSED not meaning SecurityStatus=SAFE.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Zero \neq UniversalValidator
b_rows_sample.statement: DDD warning that Zero risks becoming a 'god object' by owning detection of gaps, conflicts, type problems, temporal problems and epistemic boundaries all at once: Zero ≠ UniversalValidator. Zero is redefined narrowly as detecting epistemic boundaries/deficiencies relevant to current state and purpose, aggregating epistemic consequences of findings from separate domain validators (schema, type, policy, security violations).

b_rows_sample.anchor: LordCandidate \neq Knowledge
b_rows_sample.statement: LordCandidate ≠ Knowledge and LordCandidate ≠ Evidence: Lord can propose 'there may be a moral-obligation dimension' but it becomes knowledge only after investigation; critical to prevent AI-generated hypotheses entering the Knowledge State as facts.

b_rows_sample.anchor: S\bar{a}rathiRecommendation \neq Decision
b_rows_sample.statement: Sārathi needs a constitutional policy boundary: SārathiRecommendation ≠ Decision, SārathiAction ≠ HumanAuthorization — Sārathi may determine the next best investigation, but the Knower decides whether to accept it unless the system has explicitly delegated authority.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Sārathi: (K,U,N,\Delta,P,Role) \rightarrow Guidance
b_rows_sample.statement: Corrects Sārathi(K,I,Δ)->Action as too simplistic: Sārathi:(K,U,N,Δ,P,Role) -> Guidance, which may then produce Decision, which may then authorize Action, giving Guidance ≠ Decision ≠ Action (confirming an earlier DDD warning). Also reframes Zero/Lord/Sārathi as three functions/lenses over the state rather than three sequential stages: Zero=Diagnose, Lord=Reason/Synthesize/Orient, Sārathi=Guide, with Decision->Action occurring outside those lenses; explicitly an architectural abstraction, not a literal theological equivalence.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Sārathi: (State, Norms, Role, Context, Discrepancies) \rightarrow Guidance
b_rows_sample.statement: Revises Sārathi(K,I,Δ)->Action (too direct) to Sārathi:(State,Norms,Role,Context,Discrepancies)->Guidance -> CandidateActions -> Decision -> Action, giving proper separation of concerns. Reaffirms Zero as a pure DiagnosticFunction that must not itself decide ('therefore do X'). Corrects Lord from 'merely a reasoning engine/LLM reasoning' to AuthoritativeKnowledge+NormativeOrientation+InterpretiveResolution, since Krishna in the text functions as an authoritative source of teaching, not just an inference engine — called crucial for KnowledgeOS governance. Confirms Sārathi = ContextualGuidance, distinguishing Lord ('what is authoritative/true/normative') from Sārathi ('how does that apply here') from Decision ('what will I choose') from Action ('what will I actually do').

b_rows_sample.anchor: Zero(K,I,C,P) \rightarrow \text{Epistemic Boundaries}
b_rows_sample.statement: Reframes Zero/Lord/Sārathi as product capabilities rather than domain entities: Zero(K,I,C,P)->Epistemic Boundaries acts as an 'epistemic diagnostic engine' (missing dimensions, unknown values, missing/weak/conflicting evidence, logical contradictions, stale knowledge, contextual mismatches, unresolved questions, unsupported assumptions, Ideal-State discrepancies); Lord asks 'what else might matter?' enabling 'horizon expansion' beyond gap-checking; Sārathi:(K,I,Z,L,Q,C)->NextAction performs 'epistemic navigation', worked through a Bhīṣma-relationship example (Zero flags unknown relationship, Lord flags kinship as material, Sārathi recommends investigating it before evaluating the decision).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Can we migrate this Nexus installation?
b_rows_sample.statement: Worked example: asked 'Can we migrate this Nexus installation?', a conventional AI answers directly, while KnowledgeOS first constructs required dimensions (version, repository inventory, blob stores, storage, network, DNS, firewall, certificates, backup, dependencies, authentication, operational constraints), runs Zero to find missing items (backup verification, firewall confirmation, certificate ownership, dependency inventory), and has Sārathi respond 'Do not decide migration readiness yet. Investigate these four items.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: perform justified action given epistemic state
b_rows_sample.statement: Contrasts a conventional agent optimizing 'complete task' against KnowledgeOS optimizing 'perform justified action given epistemic state', worked through a deploy-approval example: required knowledge checklist (code reviewed✓, tests passed✓, architecture approved✓, security assessment✗, production configuration✗, rollback strategy✗) yields Zero='3 critical gaps' and Sārathi='DO NOT DEPLOY. Investigate security, configuration and rollback.' Also frames the agent loop as Understand Intent->Construct Knowledge State->Discover Dimensions->Zero->Identify Gaps/Conflicts->Lord->Expand Possible Investigation->Sārathi->Select Next Epistemic Action->Agent/Tool->Observation->Update Knowledge State->Repeat, called 'an epistemically governed autonomous agent architecture'.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Retrieve(Q,K_t,I_t,C) \rightarrow EvidenceCandidates
b_rows_sample.statement: Corrects plain Retrieve(Query)->Documents to a goal-directed Retrieve(Q,K_t,I_t,C)->EvidenceCandidates: the retrieval system 'knows why it is retrieving', discovering relevant dimensions (e.g. version, repository topology, blob stores, firewall, certificates for a migration decision) before retrieving. Zero can drive retrieval: given a partially-filled knowledge-state checklist, Zero reports specific gaps (backup verification, firewall rules, certificate ownership) and Sārathi generates a concrete investigation plan (search infrastructure docs for backup configuration, etc.), giving Zero -> Gap -> Sārathi -> Retrieval as part of the investigation loop, not a one-shot lookup.

b_rows_sample.anchor: \text{Zero}(K_t)\rightarrow\text{epistemic boundary}
b_rows_sample.statement: Zero continuously reveals 'what is still unknown' (Zero(K_t)->G_t, G_0->G_1->...); ideally G_t->∅, but if the knowledge space is genuinely unbounded Zero may never establish G_t=∅. The stronger concept is Zero(K_t)->epistemic boundary, with Moksha representing the boundary itself being transcended rather than merely all currently detected gaps being filled — judged 'much more profound'.
